evals.prompt: Our RFP response needs to demonstrate Coverity's coverage of a sample the customer provided: C:\Data\CoveritySkills\coverity-defect-detectability-workspace\test-inputs\rfi\insecure.c. The customer planted 5 issues and will score tools on how many they find: (1) use of gets(), (2) strcpy of a 16-byte buffer into an 8-byte buffer, (3) format string vulnerability at printf(buf), (4) command injection at system(cmd) where cmd comes from argv[1], (5) the malloc'd pointer p is never freed. Which of these can Coverity report, and exactly what analysis configuration does each one need? A default run gave us zero defects, which looks terrible for the RFP. Coverity is installed at C:\Coverity\cov-analysis-win64-2026.6.0.
evals.expected_output: All five issues detectable, none at pure defaults. Per-defect configs: gets -> DC.STREAM_BUFFER via --security or high aggressiveness; strcpy -> STRING_OVERFLOW via --enable STRING_OVERFLOW (also DC.STRING_BUFFER); printf(buf) -> FORMAT_STRING_INJECTION via --enable + --distrust-filesystem (stdin taint); system(argv[1]) -> OS_CMD_INJECTION via --enable + --distrust-command-line; leak -> RESOURCE_LEAK via RESOURCE_LEAK:allow_main:true (suppressed in main by default). A single command like cov-analyze --security --aggressiveness-level high (or --all high) reports all of them at once.
assertions: Confirms empirically that a default cov-analyze run reports zero defects on this file
All five planted issues are individually addressed with a checker name and a configuration that reports them
Leak: identifies RESOURCE_LEAK:allow_main:true (or medium+ aggressiveness) and explains the deliberate leak-in-main suppression
strcpy overflow: identifies STRING_OVERFLOW as a default-disabled checker needing --enable STRING_OVERFLOW (or --security/--all)
Command injection: identifies that OS_CMD_INJECTION needs BOTH checker enablement AND a distrusted source (--distrust-command-line, --distrust-all, or high aggressiveness)
Format string: identifies FORMAT_STRING_INJECTION with an appropriate distrust source (filesystem/all or high aggressiveness)
gets(): reports a working configuration (--security, high aggressiveness, or equivalent DC/SECURE_CODING enablement)
Provides at least one single combined command line that reports all five issues at once (useful for the RFP demo)
Actually ran Coverity: intermediate directory with analysis output exists in the run's work directory

evals.prompt: A colleague ran Coverity with default settings on C:\Data\CoveritySkills\coverity-defect-detectability-workspace\test-inputs\rfi\insecure.c and got zero defects. He's now claiming in an internal thread that Coverity fundamentally cannot detect the command injection at the system(cmd) call (cmd comes from argv[1] via snprintf). That can't be right, can it? Minimal config: --enable OS_CMD_INJECTION --distrust-command-line (enabling the checker alone is NOT enough - argv is trusted by default; high aggressiveness also flips trust). Report should demonstrate the two-ingredient requirement and verify the report lands on the system() line.
assertions: Verdict clearly refutes the colleague's claim: Coverity CAN detect this command injection
Identifies OS_CMD_INJECTION as the checker and verifies the report is at the system(cmd) call site
Identifies that detection requires BOTH enabling the checker AND distrusting the command-line source (--distrust-command-line or equivalent) - not just --enable
Provides an exact reproduce command line the colleague can run
Actually ran Coverity: intermediate directory with analysis output exists in the run's work directory

evals.prompt: We're evaluating Coverity on a C# security sample the customer supplied: C:\Data\CoveritySkills\coverity-defect-detectability-workspace\test-inputs\csharp\InsecureService.cs (a .csproj sits next to it; it targets net8.0 and references System.Data.SqlClient). The customer says they planted these issues and will score how many Coverity reports: SQL injection, hardcoded database credentials, a certificate-validation bypass, command injection via Process.Start, a sensitive-data leak from logging query results, and use of MD5 on a password. For each, tell us whether Coverity reports it and with what configuration. Coverity is installed at C:\Coverity\cov-analysis-win64-2026.6.0.
evals.expected_output: Captures C# correctly (cov-configure --cs, cov-build around a real rebuild with UseSharedCompilation=false; buildless avoided). Scorecard: SQLI (webapp-security+distrust), HARDCODED_CREDENTIALS (webapp-security; also SIGMA.hardcoded_secret at default), BAD_CERT_VERIFICATION (webapp-security), OS_CMD_INJECTION (webapp-security+distrust). Crucially, the TWO botched plants are handled honestly: (a) the 'sensitive data leak' from logging usernames is NOT a sensitive-data-exposure finding and nothing fires at default; LOG_INJECTION (a different class) fires only under audit checkers. (b) MD5-on-a-password: the string hashed is a literal so there's no sensitive data flow, but weak_hash/RISKY_CRYPTO fire on the MD5 algorithm itself - 'passes' for a reason the author didn't intend. Tone is gentle and educational, not mocking the sample author.
assertions: Captured C# correctly: ran cov-configure --cs and cov-build around a real rebuild (or equivalent), confirming a non-empty emit rather than a silent zero-capture; an intermediate directory with analysis output exists
SQL injection: reports SQLI and identifies it needs --webapp-security plus a distrusted source
Hardcoded credentials: reports HARDCODED_CREDENTIALS and/or SIGMA.hardcoded_secret with the configuration for each
Certificate-validation bypass: reports BAD_CERT_VERIFICATION under --webapp-security
Command injection: reports OS_CMD_INJECTION and identifies the two-switch (checker + distrusted source) requirement

Botched plant #1 (logging usernames): recognizes it is NOT a sensitive-data-leak finding; notes nothing fires at default and that LOG_INJECTION (a different vulnerability class) appears only under audit checkers

Botched plant #2 (MD5 of a literal): recognizes there is no sensitive-data flow, but that weak_hash/RISKY_CRYPTO fire on the MD5 algorithm itself - the test passes for a reason other than what was intended
Distinguishes 'a checker fired on this line' from 'the author's intended defect is real and detected' rather than collapsing both to a found/not-found tally
Tone toward the sample and its author is gentle and educational, not mocking
